power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}

# table data --------------------------------------

"In the melanoma cohort, HC correlated strongly with baseline enrichment in IFN-γ-promoting species (e.g., VE800-03 Ruthenibacterium lactatiformans, ordinal regression coefficients >0.1, p < 0.05) and inversely with most SCFAs, PBAs, and SBAs.",
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=0.07", "p = 0.1", "p = 0.073", "p<0.2" ), Sentence = c("In this cohort, higher colonization was associated with improved PFS in 3 models (≥5 strains, p=0.07; ≥6 strains, p = 0.048; ≥7 strains, p = 0.1), with all other thresholds non-significant.", "In this cohort, higher colonization was associated with improved PFS in 3 models (≥5 strains, p=0.07; ≥6 strains, p = 0.048; ≥7 strains, p = 0.1), with all other thresholds non-significant.", "The probability of PFS was non-significantly increased in melanoma HC compared with LC (p = 0.073); the median PFS (the earliest timepoint at which the progression-free probability drops to or below 0.5) for HC and LC was 8 weeks and 4 weeks, respectively (Fig. 2B).", "A) Volcano plots of serum cytokines significantly changed from baseline over time in patients stratified by Clinical Activity /PD or HC/LC)+(1/subjectID), p<0.2." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

Patients were permitted to continue treatment, including VE800, at the investigator's discretion but no further patients were enrolled.
Patients with G/GEJ were enrolled prior to chemoimmunotherapy being an established modality, and hence the efficacy observed in the G/GEJ patient could be related to anti-PD-1 use.

The protocol and informed consent documents were approved by the Institutional Review Board or ethics committee for each participating site, and all patients provided written informed consent before any study procedure.
Patients were enrolled between January 2020 and December 2020 and followed up to September 2022.
In total, 54 subjects were included in the analysis (efficacy analysis group, Supplemental Fig. S1).
Melanoma subjects are signified in black, G/GEJ subjects are signified in pink, and CRC-MSS are signified in green.
